name: Ancient History
topics: Period: New Kingdom Egypt, Amenhotep III to Ramesses II
note: Built around Pompeii and Herculaneum, Hatshepsut and New Kingdom Egypt from Amenhotep III to Ramesses II (2017 syllabus, used for HSC 2027). Dates for Egypt vary between scholars, so use the ones your teacher gives.

cards.f: When did Vesuvius erupt, and why is the date debated?
cards.b: AD 79. Pliny's letters were long read as 24 August, but autumn fruit, warm clothing and a charcoal graffito found in 2018 suggest October.

cards.f: What is our main written source for the eruption?
cards.b: Two letters from Pliny the Younger to the historian Tacitus, written about 25 years later, describing the eruption cloud and his uncle Pliny the Elder's death at Stabiae.

cards.f: Limitations of Pliny the Younger's letters as a source.
cards.b: Written decades later, from Misenum across the bay, partly to honour his uncle, and they describe Misenum and Stabiae rather than Pompeii or Herculaneum.

cards.f: Two phases of the eruption.
cards.b: The Plinian phase: a tall column dropping pumice (lapilli) and ash, mostly on Pompeii. Then the Peléan phase: pyroclastic surges and flows that killed those still there.

cards.f: How were Pompeii and Herculaneum buried differently?
cards.b: Pompeii lay under about 4 to 6 m of pumice and ash. Herculaneum was buried under about 20 m of pyroclastic material that set hard, which preserved wood, food and papyri.

cards.f: Which earthquake damaged the towns before AD 79?
cards.b: The earthquake of AD 62 (or 63), described by Seneca and Tacitus. Repairs were still underway in 79, e.g. on the Temple of Venus.

cards.f: What did the 1980s discoveries in Herculaneum's boat sheds reveal?
cards.b: About 300 skeletons of people sheltering by the shore. Earlier, few bodies had been found there, and they show that many people did not escape.

cards.f: What did Giuseppe Fiorelli contribute?
cards.b: From 1863 he poured plaster into the cavities left by decomposed bodies to make casts, and divided Pompeii into regions, insulae and doorways (still used today).

cards.f: Early excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii.
cards.b: Bourbon tunnelling at Herculaneum from 1738 and Pompeii from 1748, mainly treasure hunting for the king, with little recording.

cards.f: What was Amedeo Maiuri's contribution?
cards.b: Director from 1924 to 1961, he excavated large areas of both sites with more scientific methods and opened them to tourists, though some of his restorations are now questioned.

cards.f: What is the Villa of the Papyri?
cards.b: A luxury villa outside Herculaneum with a library of carbonised papyrus scrolls (mostly Epicurean philosophy) and many bronze statues.

cards.f: How is new technology reading the Herculaneum scrolls?
cards.b: CT scanning and machine learning (the Vesuvius Challenge, from 2023) are reading text inside scrolls too fragile to unroll.

cards.f: What do electoral programmata tell us?
cards.b: Painted election notices for duoviri and aediles show local politics, who supported candidates (including women and trade groups) and that many people could read.

cards.f: Local government in Pompeii.
cards.b: Two duoviri (senior magistrates), two aediles (public works, markets, games), and a town council (ordo decurionum) of wealthy men.

cards.f: Evidence of the economy in Pompeii.
cards.b: Bakeries (e.g. Modestus' with carbonised loaves), fulleries (Stephanus), garum production (Umbricius Scaurus), wine amphorae, thermopolia (food bars) and shops.

cards.f: What does the House of the Vettii show?
cards.b: Wealthy freedmen brothers showing off their new status with fine wall paintings, a large peristyle garden and a Priapus image at the entrance.

cards.f: What does the House of the Faun show?
cards.b: One of the largest houses, famous for the Alexander mosaic and the dancing faun statue: the wealth of Pompeii's elite.

cards.f: What does the Villa of the Mysteries show?
cards.b: A villa outside Pompeii with a large painted frieze, usually linked to Dionysian rites or a bride's initiation into marriage.

cards.f: Evidence of religion in the cities.
cards.b: Temples of Apollo, Venus, Jupiter and Isis, household shrines (lararia), the imperial cult (the Augustales), and tombs along roads outside the gates.

cards.f: What does the Temple of Isis show?
cards.b: Eastern cults were popular. It was rebuilt after the 62 earthquake by Numerius Popidius Celsinus, a freedman's son, to win his family status.

cards.f: What was the AD 59 amphitheatre riot?
cards.b: A fight between Pompeians and Nucerians at games in Pompeii. Tacitus says the Senate banned games there for ten years; a wall painting shows the riot.

cards.f: Entertainment and leisure in Pompeii.
cards.b: The amphitheatre (gladiators), the large and small theatres, the palaestra, and the public baths (Stabian, Forum and Central).

cards.f: What do the skeletons tell us about the people?
cards.b: Age, sex, height, diet (fish, grain), health (dental problems, injuries) and occupations, from studies such as Estelle Lazer's (Pompeii) and Sara Bisel's (Herculaneum).

cards.f: Main conservation threats at the sites.
cards.b: Weather, vegetation, tourism (millions of visitors), earlier poor restorations, theft and underfunding. The Great Pompeii Project (from 2012) and Herculaneum Conservation Project respond to them.

cards.f: Ethical issues at Pompeii and Herculaneum.
cards.b: Displaying human remains, balancing tourism with conservation, whether to excavate the remaining unexcavated areas, and how much to reconstruct.

cards.f: Role of women in Pompeii.
cards.b: Some wealthy women owned property and businesses and funded buildings, e.g. Eumachia (the Building of Eumachia) and Julia Felix, who rented out parts of her estate.

cards.f: Why are freedmen important in the evidence?
cards.b: Former slaves could gain wealth and status as Augustales and benefactors, e.g. the Vettii brothers and Popidius Celsinus' family.

cards.f: Hatshepsut's family background.
cards.b: Daughter of Thutmose I and Queen Ahmose, wife of her half-brother Thutmose II, mother of Neferure, and stepmother and aunt of Thutmose III. 18th dynasty.

cards.f: How did Hatshepsut come to rule?
cards.b: When Thutmose II died, the young Thutmose III became king with Hatshepsut as regent. By about year 7 she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh and ruled as senior co-ruler.

cards.f: Approximate dates of her reign.
cards.b: About 1479 to 1458 BC (dates vary by chronology), roughly 20 years counted from Thutmose III's accession.

cards.f: Title she held as queen that helped her rise.
cards.b: God's Wife of Amun, a powerful religious office that gave her wealth, a household and links to the priesthood of Amun.

cards.f: How did Hatshepsut justify her kingship?
cards.b: The divine birth scenes at Deir el-Bahri (Amun as her father), the coronation inscription claiming Thutmose I chose her, and her building and religious works.

cards.f: How is Hatshepsut shown in her statues?
cards.b: Early statues show her as a woman. Later ones show her with the male king's body, kilt, nemes headcloth and false beard, fitting the traditional image of a pharaoh.

cards.f: What is Djeser-Djeseru?
cards.b: Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri ('Holy of Holies'), terraced against the cliffs, with reliefs of the divine birth and the Punt expedition.

cards.f: Who was Senenmut?
cards.b: Her chief official and steward, tutor of Neferure and probably the architect of Deir el-Bahri. His closeness to her is much debated.

cards.f: Other key officials of Hatshepsut.
cards.b: Hapuseneb (High Priest of Amun), Nehesy (Chancellor, led the Punt expedition), Thutiy (treasurer, temple fittings) and Ineni (architect).

cards.f: What was the expedition to Punt?
cards.b: A trade expedition by sea, probably to the East African coast, bringing back incense trees, myrrh, gold, ebony and exotic animals. It is shown on the walls of Deir el-Bahri.

cards.f: Building works at Karnak.
cards.b: Two pairs of obelisks (one still stands), the eighth pylon, and the Red Chapel (Chapelle Rouge) for Amun's sacred boat.

cards.f: What does the Speos Artemidos inscription say?
cards.b: A rock-cut temple text where Hatshepsut claims she restored order and temples left ruined by the Hyksos.

cards.f: Evidence of military activity under Hatshepsut.
cards.b: Limited: references to a campaign in Nubia, possibly in Sinai and the Levant. She is not mainly remembered for war.

cards.f: What happened to her monuments after her death?
cards.b: Late in Thutmose III's reign (about 20 years after her death) her images and names were removed or replaced, and her obelisks were walled in.

cards.f: Why were her monuments attacked? Main views.
cards.b: Older views: personal hatred by Thutmose III. Most scholars now think it was political: to secure the succession for his son Amenhotep II and restore the 'proper' male line, since it happened so late.

cards.f: How was her mummy identified?
cards.b: In 2007 a mummy from tomb KV60 was linked to her through a tooth matching a gap in a box bearing her name (Zahi Hawass). Some scholars still question it.

cards.f: Evaluate Hatshepsut's significance.
cards.b: A rare female pharaoh who ruled successfully for about 20 years: peace, trade and major building. Her erasure shows how unusual her rule was seen to be.

cards.f: Who was Amenhotep III and why was his reign significant?
cards.b: An 18th-dynasty king (about 1390 to 1352 BC) whose long peaceful reign was a high point of wealth, diplomacy and building.

cards.f: Queen Tiye's importance.
cards.b: Amenhotep III's chief wife, of non-royal birth, influential in diplomacy; foreign rulers wrote to her in the Amarna letters.

cards.f: Building works of Amenhotep III.
cards.b: The Colossi of Memnon (his mortuary temple), Luxor temple, the Malkata palace in Thebes, and work at Karnak and Soleb in Nubia.

cards.f: What are the Amarna letters?
cards.b: Clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform: diplomatic letters between Egypt and Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites, Assyria and Canaanite vassals, under Amenhotep III and Akhenaten.

cards.f: What did the Amarna letters show about foreign policy?
cards.b: Egypt kept peace with great powers through gifts and royal marriages (e.g. with Mitanni), while vassal rulers in Canaan asked for help against rivals.

cards.f: Akhenaten's religious changes.
cards.b: He promoted the Aten (the sun disc) above all gods, closed temples of Amun and erased Amun's name, and changed his name from Amenhotep IV.

cards.f: Where was Akhetaten?
cards.b: Akhenaten's new capital at modern Amarna, built in his year 5 to 6 and abandoned soon after his death.

cards.f: What is distinctive about Amarna art?
cards.b: Informal family scenes with the Aten's rays ending in hands, and elongated faces and bodies for the king and royal family.

cards.f: Nefertiti's role.
cards.b: Akhenaten's chief queen, shown with unusual prominence in worship and even smiting enemies; she may have ruled briefly after him.

cards.f: What did Tutankhamun's reign do?
cards.b: He changed his name from Tutankhaten, moved the court back, and restored Amun's temples and priests (the Restoration Stela).

cards.f: Who were Ay and Horemheb?
cards.b: Kings after Tutankhamun. Horemheb, an army commander, restored order and issued a decree against corruption, and later kings erased the Amarna kings from king lists.

cards.f: How did the 19th dynasty begin?
cards.b: Horemheb named his vizier and general Ramesses I as heir. His son Seti I followed, restoring Egypt's power in the Levant.

cards.f: Seti I's achievements.
cards.b: Campaigns in Canaan and Syria (Karnak hypostyle hall reliefs), his temple at Abydos with the Abydos King List, and a fine tomb in the Valley of the Kings.

cards.f: What happened at the Battle of Kadesh?
cards.b: About 1274 BC, in Ramesses II's year 5, against the Hittite king Muwatalli II in Syria. Ramesses' army was ambushed; the result was a draw, though he presented it as a great victory.

cards.f: What did the Hittite peace treaty establish?
cards.b: About 1259 BC, Ramesses II and Hattusili III agreed peace, a mutual defence alliance and the return of fugitives. Copies survive in both Egyptian and Hittite versions.

cards.f: Ramesses II's building program.
cards.b: Abu Simbel in Nubia, the Ramesseum, the new capital Pi-Ramesses in the delta, Karnak's hypostyle hall and additions at Luxor.

cards.f: How did Ramesses II present himself as pharaoh?
cards.b: As a warrior and god-like king through huge statues, Kadesh reliefs on many temples, deification in Nubia, and long rule (about 66 years) with many children.

cards.f: Who were the Hittites?
cards.b: A powerful kingdom in Anatolia (modern Turkey) that competed with Egypt for control of Syria during the New Kingdom.

cards.f: What role did the army play in the New Kingdom?
cards.b: Standing professional army with chariots, used to keep an empire in Nubia and the Levant. Military men rose to the throne (Horemheb, Ramesses I).

cards.f: Why was Nubia important to New Kingdom Egypt?
cards.b: Gold, ivory, ebony and soldiers. It was ruled by the King's Son of Kush (viceroy), and temples such as Abu Simbel showed Egyptian power there.

cards.f: Where are Pompeii and Herculaneum, and how did they differ?
cards.b: Both on the Bay of Naples near Vesuvius. Pompeii was a busy commercial town of about 10 000 to 12 000 people; Herculaneum was a smaller, wealthier seaside town of about 4000 to 5000.

cards.f: Layout of Pompeii.
cards.b: Walls with seven gates, a grid of streets, the forum as the civic and religious centre, the amphitheatre and palaestra in the south-east, and tombs along the roads outside the gates.

cards.f: What was in the forum at Pompeii?
cards.b: Temple of Jupiter, basilica (law courts and business), macellum (market), Building of Eumachia, comitium (voting), the municipal offices and the Temple of Vespasian.

cards.f: What does the Herculaneum Augustales building tell us?
cards.b: Freedmen priests of the imperial cult had their own meeting hall with fine paintings: a route to status for wealthy ex-slaves.

cards.f: Evidence for slavery at the sites.
cards.b: Slave quarters and a slaves' room found in a villa at Civita Giuliana (2021), shackles, inscriptions naming slaves, and skeletons such as the 'slave' at Herculaneum with heavy wear on the bones.

cards.f: Street features in Pompeii.
cards.b: Raised pavements, stepping stones across the roads, deep cart ruts, public fountains at crossroads and lead pipes from the castellum aquae (water tower) by the Vesuvius Gate.

cards.f: Water supply in the cities.
cards.b: An aqueduct branch brought water to the castellum aquae, then lead pipes fed public fountains, baths and wealthy houses. Earlier, cisterns collected rain from the impluvium.

cards.f: Parts of a typical atrium house.
cards.b: Fauces (entrance), atrium with impluvium under the compluvium, tablinum (reception), cubicula (bedrooms), triclinium (dining room), peristyle garden, kitchen and latrine.

cards.f: The four Pompeian painting styles.
cards.b: First: painted imitation marble blocks. Second: architectural scenes with depth. Third: flat panels with delicate ornament and small pictures. Fourth: a mix of the previous styles, often with theatrical frames and mythological scenes.

cards.f: What were thermopolia?
cards.b: Food and drink bars with counters holding dolia (jars). Pompeii had about 80, showing many people ate out. A well-preserved one with painted food was excavated in Regio V in 2020.

cards.f: What do the Praedia of Julia Felix show?
cards.b: A large property where the owner rented out baths, shops, an inn and apartments: women could own and run businesses.

cards.f: What was found at the Lupanar?
cards.b: A purpose-built brothel with stone beds, erotic paintings and graffiti naming prostitutes and customers.

cards.f: How was food produced around the cities?
cards.b: Vineyards and farms on the slopes of Vesuvius; the Villa Regina at Boscoreale shows a working wine farm. Wilhelmina Jashemski's root casts identified the vines and trees in Pompeii's gardens.

cards.f: Religion: household worship.
cards.b: Family shrines (lararia) with painted Lares, the genius of the paterfamilias and a serpent, found in kitchens and atria of most houses.

cards.f: What foreign religions appear in the evidence?
cards.b: The Egyptian cult of Isis (temple and Isiac imagery), Dionysus/Bacchus (Villa of the Mysteries), Sabazius, and possibly Judaism and Christianity (a 'Christianos' graffito, debated).

cards.f: How did the AD 62 earthquake affect the economy?
cards.b: Some wealthy families left and freedmen bought up property; repairs continued for 17 years, so many public buildings were still damaged in 79.

cards.f: Who are key modern researchers on the human remains?
cards.b: Estelle Lazer (Pompeii skeletons: a cross-section of the population, not only the old and weak) and Sara Bisel (Herculaneum boat shed skeletons: diet, health, occupations).

cards.f: What does Andrew Wallace-Hadrill argue about the cities?
cards.b: That Roman houses mixed rich and poor and work and home across the city, rather than having separate rich and poor districts. He also leads the Herculaneum Conservation Project.

cards.f: Role of the Packard Humanities Institute at Herculaneum.
cards.b: Since 2001 it has funded the Herculaneum Conservation Project with the Italian authorities, drying the site, fixing drainage and roofs, and conserving rather than excavating.

cards.f: Recent discoveries at Pompeii (Regio V and after).
cards.b: From 2018: the Street of Balconies, the House of Leda and the Swan, the fresco of Priapus, the thermopolium, charioteer and horses at Civita Giuliana, and the 2023 'pizza' still life fresco.

cards.f: Why was the Casa dei Casti Amanti excavation significant?
cards.b: Opened in 2024, it shows how excavation now goes with conservation and public display, and found a bakery where enslaved workers and a donkey were confined.

cards.f: Ethical question: should the casts be displayed?
cards.b: Casts contain real human bones. Some argue for respectful display and research; others see them as a spectacle. Recent policy treats them as human remains, with scientific study and limited display.

cards.f: Ethical question: should more of Pompeii be excavated?
cards.b: About a third is unexcavated. Leaving it protects remains for better future methods, while targeted digs (Regio V) stop slopes collapsing and give new evidence.

cards.f: What is the Great Pompeii Project?
cards.b: An EU-funded program from 2012 (about 105 million euros) to stabilise structures after the 2010 collapse of the House of the Gladiators, with Massimo Osanna as director.

cards.f: What is the Deir el-Bahri Punt relief useful for?
cards.b: It shows the ships, the Puntite chief Parehu and his wife Ati, incense trees carried in baskets, and the goods brought back: evidence of trade, propaganda and Egyptian views of foreigners.

cards.f: What did Hatshepsut claim about her monuments at Karnak?
cards.b: On her obelisks she says she made them for her father Amun, sheathed in electrum, and that future people should not say her words are boasts.

cards.f: How did Hatshepsut treat Thutmose III during her reign?
cards.b: He was co-ruler, shown behind her in reliefs, led the army, and was never removed. She dated her reign by his regnal years.

cards.f: What is the Chapelle Rouge and why does it matter?
cards.b: A red quartzite bark shrine at Karnak. Its blocks were reused and reassembled in the 1990s; they show her coronation, Opet festival and oracle of Amun.

cards.f: What was the Beautiful Festival of the Valley?
cards.b: A Theban festival where Amun's statue crossed the river to visit the mortuary temples. Deir el-Bahri was a key stop, linking Hatshepsut to Amun.

cards.f: Evidence for Hatshepsut's building beyond Thebes.
cards.b: Speos Artemidos at Beni Hasan, a temple at Buhen in Nubia, work at Hermopolis, and quarrying at Aswan and Sinai (Serabit el-Khadim).

cards.f: What was Hatshepsut's throne name?
cards.b: Maatkare, 'Maat is the ka of Re', stressing her role in keeping maat (order and truth).

cards.f: What did Senenmut's tombs show?
cards.b: He had two tombs (TT71 and TT353, the second under Deir el-Bahri with an astronomical ceiling) and about 25 statues, some holding Neferure: unusual wealth for a non-royal.

cards.f: What happened to Senenmut?
cards.b: He disappears from the record around year 16 to 19. His images in TT353 were later attacked, but it is unclear whether he fell from favour or simply died.

cards.f: How do modern historians evaluate Hatshepsut? Examples.
cards.b: Gardiner saw her as a usurper backed by officials; Tyldesley and Robins see a capable ruler who used traditional means; Dorman argued the erasure was political and late.

cards.f: Why might Hatshepsut have sent the Punt expedition?
cards.b: To restore trade links lost in the Hyksos period, to obtain myrrh for Amun's temples, and to show divine approval and prosperity under her rule.

cards.f: Was Hatshepsut's reign militarily inactive?
cards.b: Not entirely: inscriptions at Sehel and Tombos suggest a Nubian campaign, and Deir el-Bahri shows Nubian captives; but her reign is remembered for peace and building.

cards.f: Who was Yuya?
cards.b: A high official under Amenhotep III and father of Queen Tiye; his tomb (KV46) with wife Tjuyu was one of the best preserved before Tutankhamun's.

cards.f: What are the commemorative scarabs of Amenhotep III?
cards.b: Large scarabs issued to record events: his marriage to Tiye, lion and bull hunts, and the arrival of the Mitannian princess Gilukhepa.

cards.f: Why did Amenhotep III celebrate sed festivals?
cards.b: Jubilees in years 30, 34 and 37 renewing his kingship; he was increasingly shown as a god, and Malkata was built for the celebrations.

cards.f: What was Akhenaten's early reign like?
cards.b: At Karnak he built temples to the Aten with colossal statues in a new exaggerated style, while still Amenhotep IV; the move to Akhetaten came in year 5.

cards.f: What is the Great Hymn to the Aten?
cards.b: A text in Ay's Amarna tomb praising the Aten as the sole creator; often compared with Psalm 104. It shows only the king (and Nefertiti) could approach the god.

cards.f: Boundary stelae of Akhetaten.
cards.b: Rock stelae marking the city's limits, recording the king's vow never to extend the city beyond them.

cards.f: Who was Smenkhkare?
cards.b: A short-lived ruler at the end of Akhenaten's reign, possibly a brother or son, or perhaps Nefertiti under another name (Ankhkheperure).

cards.f: What happened to foreign policy under Akhenaten?
cards.b: The Amarna letters show vassals in Canaan asking for help against the Habiru and the Hittites; Egypt's influence in Syria weakened as the Hittites under Suppiluliuma expanded.

cards.f: What was the Zannanza affair?
cards.b: After Tutankhamun's death a royal widow (probably Ankhesenamun) asked the Hittite king for a son to marry. Prince Zannanza was sent but killed on the way, worsening Egyptian-Hittite relations.

cards.f: Horemheb's Edict.
cards.b: A decree against corruption by officials and soldiers (seizing boats, cattle and slaves), with harsh penalties: restoring order after Amarna.

cards.f: What were the Sea Peoples and why do they matter later?
cards.b: Groups attacking the eastern Mediterranean in the late Bronze Age. Ramesses II fought the Sherden and used them as mercenaries; Ramesses III defeated them later.

cards.f: Ramesses II's family.
cards.b: Chief wives Nefertari (temple at Abu Simbel, tomb QV66) and Isetnofret, later a Hittite princess (Maathorneferure); over 100 children, including Khaemwaset and his successor Merenptah.

cards.f: What is the Kadesh 'Poem' and 'Bulletin'?
cards.b: Two official accounts of the battle carved on temples (Abu Simbel, Luxor, Ramesseum, Abydos). They present Ramesses saving the army alone with Amun's help.

cards.f: Where was Pi-Ramesses and why was it built?
cards.b: In the eastern Delta near Avaris, close to the Levant for campaigning and trade, and the home region of the 19th dynasty.

cards.f: What role did the vizier play in New Kingdom government?
cards.b: Chief administrator under the king; two viziers (north and south) ran justice, taxation and building. Rekhmire's tomb records the duties.

cards.f: What does the tomb of Rekhmire show?
cards.b: Tribute scenes from Punt, Nubia, Crete (Keftiu) and Syria, and the 'Installation of the Vizier' text on the vizier's duties.
